replies.inference: The seriousness of the errors makes nonintervention harder to explain under theism even without attributing contradictions directly to God.

replies.title: William Lane Craig vs Michael Nugent — Does God Exist?
replies.speaker: William Lane Craig
replies.claim: Foreknowledge does not logically make a future action necessary.
replies.warrant: Craig distinguishes necessarily, if God foreknows an act it occurs, from if God foreknows it, the act occurs necessarily.
replies.inference: The fatalist conclusion is said to commit a modal fallacy.

source_span.excerpt: said if God is omniscient it precludes human freedom I spent seven years studying the relationship between Divine foreknowledge and human freedom and the argument for a theological fatalism is simply logically fallacious to say that necessarily because God foreknows x x will happen and that God foreknows acts therefore necessarily X will happen commits a fallacy in modal logic so if he's going to defend fatalism he needs to show us how his reasoning doesn't commit that logical error

replies.public_paraphrase: Craig distinguishes the necessity of the conditional from the necessity of the foreknown act, arguing that infallible knowledge does not itself make free action necessary.
replies.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Craig identifies the classic modal error cleanly: from necessarily, if God foreknows an act then it occurs, one cannot infer that the act itself occurs necessarily merely because it is foreknown. Principal limitation: Correcting that inference answers only Nugent’s no-freedom branch and does not address why an all-good creator knowingly actualizes a world containing agents whose freely chosen evil is infallibly foreseen before agents are created, a moral question distinct from their freedom. Live burden: Nugent must reformulate any fatalist case without transferring necessity across the conditional, while Craig still owes a moral account of intentional creation under complete foreknowledge. Locked score: 84/100 rewards a precise and decisive logical correction, with the score stopping short of higher because a distinct branch of Nugent’s dilemma remains unanswered.

target_evidence.public_paraphrase: Nugent argues that infallible foreknowledge leaves either no human freedom or a creator knowingly choosing agents whose future evil is already certain.
target_evidence.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Nugent frames two different moral pressures rather than relying solely on fatalism: either foreknown action is unfree, or God knowingly creates free agents whose evil choices and consequences are fully anticipated. Principal limitation: The first branch slides from certainty to necessity without defending that modal move, while the second does not show that knowingly permitting foreseeable wrongdoing is incompatible with morally sufficient reasons, freedom, or compensating goods. Live burden: Craig must answer the knowingly-created-evil branch as well as the modal branch; Nugent must demonstrate contradiction or adverse probability rather than assuming foreknowledge causally determines action. Locked score: 71/100 recognizes a legitimate moral question about creation under omniscience, but its compressed dilemma leaves both freedom and justification underanalyzed.

target_evidence.public_paraphrase: Schmid observes that lacking a property can make a foundation unlimited regarding it, so absence of limitation cannot entail maximal goodness or perfection.
target_evidence.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Schmid identifies an equivocation in the unlimitedness inference, because something can lack a finite ceiling by lacking the property altogether, leaving no route from unrestrictedness to maximal goodness, knowledge, or power. Principal limitation: The argument establishes a gap but does not exclude reasons for thinking the necessary foundation possesses the relevant properties before their magnitudes are considered, which Jones could attempt through explanatory scope. Live burden: Schmid must show that Jones’s independent appeals to consciousness, value, and cosmic order do not first establish property possession strongly enough for an anti-limit principle to support maximality. Locked score: The score of 90 appropriately marks the debate’s strongest move for its coherence, warrant, responsiveness, precision, and pressure on the central perfection bridge, tempered only by the possibility of independent property-establishing arguments.

bridges.title: Philip Goff vs Joe Folley: Consciousness, Mystical Experience, and Fine-Tuning
bridges.speaker: Philip Goff
bridges.claim: Evil and suffering count against unrestricted divine power; Goff instead holds that God made the best universe possible within divine limits.
bridges.inference: Pervasive suffering presses against an all-powerful God; if God instead made the best universe within limits, that pressure does not require abandoning every theistic interpretation.

bridges.public_paraphrase: Goff treats widespread suffering as evidence against unrestricted divine power, proposing instead that God made the best possible universe within limits; this preserves a qualified theism.
bridges.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Suffering motivates abandoning unrestricted divine power, showing how Goff’s qualified theism responds to an acknowledged objection rather than ignoring it. Principal limitation: Limiting divine power can accommodate suffering but remains underdescribed because the relevant constraints are unspecified, and calling this universe the best available does not demonstrate what alternatives were possible or why particular harms were unavoidable. Live burden: A developed account must identify independently motivated limitations and explain their consequences for suffering and fine-tuning, so the adjustment does more than protect benevolence by redefining divine capabilities around whatever world is observed. Locked score: 78 credits explicit engagement with suffering and rejection of unrestricted omnipotence, while restricting explanatory credit because the proposed limits and best-available-world judgment receive no independent substantiation in this brief account of Goff’s theological position.

bridges.title: Trent Horn vs Dan Barker — Does the Christian God Exist?
bridges.speaker: Trent Horn
bridges.claim: Jesus' bodily resurrection is the best explanation of early Christian testimony and the empty-tomb tradition.
bridges.warrant: Paul reports individual, group, and skeptical witnesses; Jewish expectations disfavored a resurrected failed messiah; group experience, Paul's prior hostility, access to a Jerusalem tomb, and women as discoverers are offered against hallucination or invention.
bridges.inference: The generic divine cause is identified with the Christian God.

source_span.excerpt: But how do we know this God is the Christian God? What if this cause is the God of another religion? The gods of ancient mythologies are limited in existence, goodness, power, and knowledge, so they can't be the true God. The true God could only be the God of classical monotheism, like Islam, Judaism, or Christianity. But if Jesus rose from the dead, then this shows the God of Christianity exists, because other religions deny Jesus rose from the dead. Antony Flew, who was at one time one of the most famous atheists in the 20th century, said the evidence for the resurrection is better than proclaimed miracles in any other religion. It's outstandingly different in quality and quantity. Even radical skeptics do not deny that Paul knew the apostles, and describe in 1 Corinthians 15 how both individuals and groups of people, as well as skeptics like himself, saw Jesus after his death. In addition, these first Christians believed Jesus rose from the dead in a Jewish society that believed dead messiahs were failed imposters, who, along with everyone else, would not rise until the end of the world. The best explanation for why Jesus' disciples preached Jesus' bodily resurrection, in defiance of these cultural norms, was because it really happened. But perhaps the apostles merely had a grief-induced hallucination. That's what Dan suggests in his writings. But there are four reasons that count against this hypothesis. One, groups of people saw Jesus, and groups of people don't have the exact same hallucination. Two, Paul was a persecutor of the church, so he would not have had any grief over the death of Jesus from which to hallucinate. Three, Jesus was buried in Jerusalem. The apostles could check his tomb to see if he really was dead, and the authorities could trot out his corpse in order to quash this new religious movement. Four, the apostles did check, and the tomb was empty. The gospel's descriptions of women discovering the empty tomb is a detail that is so embarrassing in a patriarchal society that its inclusion in the narrative only makes sense if that is just what really happened.

bridges.public_paraphrase: Because early testimony reports appearances and an empty tomb despite contrary expectations, Jesus’ bodily resurrection best explains the evidence and identifies the divine cause as Christian.
bridges.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Horn supplies the indispensable bridge from generic theism to Christianity through a clear abductive case involving Paul, group appearances, hostile prior disposition, Jewish expectations, Jerusalem burial, and women discovering the tomb. Principal limitation: The presentation treats historical materials as more settled and independent than demonstrated, leaves its best-explanation standard unspecified, and attributes a shared grief-hallucination proposal that Barker later distinguishes from his actual alternative. Live burden: The move directly bears the affirmative Christian burden because bodily resurrection would identify the earlier divine cause, but reported experiences and tomb tradition require comparison against natural and legendary explanations. Locked score: 77 is warranted because the evidence is specific, organized, and highly material, while the inference remains nondeductive and its source reliability, independence, and treatment of rival hypotheses receive compressed support.

bridges.title: Stephen Meyer vs Peter Atkins — Intelligent Design and Science
bridges.speaker: Stephen Meyer
bridges.claim: Intelligent design is presented as an inference from biological data rather than a deduction from scripture.
bridges.warrant: Meyer contrasts creationism's use of religious authority with causal reasoning he says is also used by other scientists.
bridges.inference: Religious implications do not by themselves disqualify the design inference from scientific status.

bridges.public_paraphrase: Meyer distinguishes intelligent design’s claimed inference from biological data and causal comparison from creationist deductions grounded in scriptural authority.
bridges.existing_critique: Strongest feature: Meyer clearly separates an argument’s evidential basis from its possible worldview implications, directly answering the charge that intelligent design is simply biblical creationism in scientific dress. Principal limitation: Showing that an argument begins from biological data does not validate its causal premises, and the repeated assertion that information always arises from intelligence still requires the comparative support challenged elsewhere. Live burden: He must demonstrate that the data-to-design inference survives ordinary scientific scrutiny, rather than relying on the accurate but limited point that religious implications do not by themselves disqualify a hypothesis. Locked score: 81/100 because the distinction is precise, relevant, and methodologically important, although it mostly clarifies status rather than adding new causal evidence.
